headline: Peconic Pushes Into the Upper 70s — Porgies Pile Up at Shelter Island While Bass Go Nocturnal
subhead: The bay's running its full August pattern now — thick scup on the bottom, fluke scattered but real in the channels, and stripers only showing themselves after dark.
body_markdown:
The Peconic runs on its own clock, and every August it hits the same stride — full heat, slack afternoons, and a bottom bite that doesn't care what the sun's doing. This bay warms faster than the Sound every spring, and by the first week of August it's paying that heat back with interest. We're deep into the upper 70s in the coves and flats now, warmer in the skinny water off Hashamomuck and Cornelius Point, and that heat has pushed the whole system into its classic midsummer rhythm — porgies thick on structure, fluke working the channels on the moving tide, and the resident stripers sliding down onto deep structure to sit out the daylight hours.

Shelter Island is doing exactly what it does this time of year. I fished the Route 114 bridge rip on the last of an outgoing tide Wednesday morning and it was about as textbook a porgy session as you'll get — 15 to 20 feet of water, high-low rigs with size 4 hooks, sandworm and skimmer clam, and fish stacked so thick you'd mark bait balls on the bottom before the anchor even set. Cornelius Point and the Fleet's Neck side are holding the same class of fish — mostly 12 to 14 inches with enough 15s mixed in to make it worth culling. Coecles Harbor has been quietly good too if you want to get away from boat traffic. Crushed clam chum off the stern turns a decent bite into a steady one — the scup follow that scent trail up in the water column and you'll start picking off fish mid-column instead of dead bottom.

Fluke are a different story this week — present, but scattered, and you have to work for them. The North Race off Robins Island and the channel edges between Nassau Point and the island have been the most consistent, 25 to 35 feet, drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, slow and dragging bottom on the outgoing. I'm getting keepers in that spread — nothing over 22 inches, but a few solid teens mixed with shorts most drifts. Jessup Neck has been softer, more shorts than keepers, which tells me the bigger fish have pushed into deeper water as the surface temps climbed. If you're marking bait but not getting bit, try slowing the drift down even further — with the water this warm, fluke aren't chasing anything fast.

Stripers have settled into the pattern we called out a couple weeks back — as the tides softened toward the neap, bass would compress into the strongest current windows and the deepest, coolest structure, and that's exactly what's playing out at Plum Gut and Orient Point right now. Daytime, forget it unless you're jigging deep on structure — the fish are down on the bottom of the Gut in that hard current, uninterested in anything but a vertical presentation right on their nose. But after dark, eels fished on the last of the ebb around the Gut and under the bridges at Shelter Island have been producing solid fish in the high 20s to low 30s. First light is the other window — bucktails worked along the rip edges at Orient Point before the sun gets up high enough to push the fish back down.

Bluefish are following the bunker, plain and simple, and right now those schools are moving through Gardiners Bay unevenly — some mornings you find blitzing fish off Gull Pond and near Orient, other mornings the bay's dead calm with nothing showing. When you find the bunker, it's fast and violent — poppers and 2-ounce metal at first light, don't overthink it. When you don't find bunker, don't waste your morning searching blind — check the birds first.

Weakfish are still a bonus fish rather than a target, but they're around. Hashamomuck's protected cove has given up a few solid weakfish on the outgoing tide working bucktail tipped with a strip of squid along the sand/shell bottom, and South Jamesport Beach on the north fork side has been holding the same mixed bag — weakfish, porgy, and the occasional keeper fluke working the beach on that same outgoing push. Both are good family spots if you want an evening on the sand instead of a boat day — just mind Hashamomuck's day-use hours if you're planning an early start.

We're heading into the neap around August 5-6, and that's going to soften current through the Gut and the connecting cuts even further over the next few days. That's typically the window where I slow everything down — lighter bucktails, longer pauses, more patience on the drift — and it tends to produce a few bonus fluke that the faster tides pushed off the structure. I'd focus the next week on early and late sessions: porgies at first light off Shelter Island while the water's still cool enough to have them shallow, then fluke on the slower afternoon drifts through the channels, and save the last hour of daylight and the first couple hours of dark for stripers at the Gut. If the bunker schools hold in Gardiners Bay, check them daily — that bite can turn on and off within the same tide.
